#6206. Qatar-Gifted 747 Air Force One Claims 2 Records On 15-Hour Nonstop Flight From China

The Qatari-gifted Boeing 747-8, now flying as the VC-25B Bridge aircraft, set two Air Force records on its return from Shenzhen, China, according to the White House. The jet reportedly made the heaviest takeoff in Air Force history at just under one million pounds, and also flew the longest nonstop Air Force One flight to date, lasting nearly 15 hours.

The aircraft left Shenzhen at 5:54 PM local time on November 19 and landed at Joint Base Andrews at 8:01 PM local time with no refueling stop, carrying President Donald Trump home from the APEC summit. The jet cruised at 33,000 feet and averaged 500 knots (926 km/h), passing over Shanghai, Tokyo, Shemya, Winnipeg, and Cleveland. Trump put the duration at about 14.5 hours and said the trip normally takes closer to 20 with a fuel stop, which he credited to newer equipment.

The 747-8i on which the VC-25B is based has a maximum takeoff weight of 987,000 pounds (447,694 kg), which TWZ notes exceeds that of a fully loaded C-5M Galaxy, and an endurance of 15 to 16 hours is commonly quoted for the type. The 7,500 nautical miles (13,890 km) flown sits inside the nearly 7,800 nautical miles (14,446 km) Boeing lists for a commercial 747-8i.

That comparison has limits. The Bridge jet is probably much lighter than a fully loaded airliner even with maximum fuel, although extra tanks may have been added during conversion, so its true maximum range remains unclear. The records therefore show the airframe operating near the upper edge of its envelope, not beyond what the type was designed to do.

According to a card handed to the accompanying press pool:

"The VC-25B conducted the heaviest takeoff in Air Force history, at just under one million pounds, and completed the longest nonstop Air Force One sortie to date, at nearly 15 hours."

The Bridge jet cannot be refueled in flight, and neither can the two purpose-built VC-25Bs that Boeing is under contract to deliver. TWZ reports that the requirement was dropped in 2017 as a cost-cutting measure, and that the new E-4C command post aircraft, built on the same 747 model, will keep the capability. The two aging VC-25As can take on fuel in the air, though only in emergencies, and they stopped in Alaska to refuel on the way home from this trip.

Range requirements add to the concern. The original VC-25B requirement was roughly 7,100 nautical miles (13,149 km), later revised to 5,900 (10,927 km), while the Air Force fact sheet lists about 6,800 (12,594 km) for the VC-25A. TWZ concludes that unless the new jets exceed the revised figure by a wide margin, they cannot fly this route nonstop, and it points to the weight of nuclear hardening, defenses, and tailored systems as the likely cause.

Simple Flying puts the cost of the VC-25B program at $5.3 billion, driven by protection against electromagnetic pulses, missile evasion, and secure global communications. TWZ adds that time aloft is central to continuity of government planning.

A gifted 747-8 heads overseas amid secret plane swaps and unconfirmed countermeasures that leave experts uneasy.

The mission also brought all three presidential 747s to Asia. The Bridge jet, painted in the red, white, and blue livery Trump has favored, carried the president, while the older VC-25As, registered 82-8000 and 92-9000, accompanied it, and all three were seen together in Manila. A second aircraft routinely travels as a mechanical backup, but it is not known whether the third jet continued to China.

The Bridge aircraft arrived at Joint Base Andrews on June 19, intended to serve until the long-term VC-25B is delivered. It debuted as Air Force One on July 1, flying the president to North Dakota, and the Air Force accepted it less than two months before that. L3Harris completed the conversion in 10 months, and TWZ says significant questions remain about whether the jet can support the full range of mission requirements, though officials and the contractor say concerns have been addressed.

The final modification cost is undisclosed, with an earlier estimate of under $400 million. Analysts had speculated that the interim jet was unsuited to international missions because of its limited modifications, a view the recent China trip undercuts. The VC-25Bs are expected in 2028, and the VC-25As are scheduled to retire in 2029.

#6205. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

#6204. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:

What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

When they fly first class, they want this…

It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:

Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:

If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):

I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:

At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The issue is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service…

What’s your take on the possible merit of US carriers offering first class?

#6203. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6202. Can Microsoft Flight Simulator Really Teach You To Fly A Boeing 737 Or An Airbus A320?

Microsoft Flight Simulator cannot fully train someone to fly a Boeing 737 or an Airbus A320 on its own, but its impressively authentic geography, weather, and avionics have made it a popular pilot training tool to supplement many levels of flight school. Although a home setup lacks the motion feedback and entire flight deck of a certified airline simulator, MSFS' high-fidelity interface, physics, plane attributes, and environment provide users with a realistic cockpit atmosphere.

MSFS simulates airflow across hundreds of airframe points, whereas third-party add-ons recreate Garmin G1000 glass cockpits, navigation radios, and aircraft flight management systems down to individual electrical circuits. Its combination of great system accuracy and little tactile input makes home simulation ideal for instrument flight instruction. Student pilots and hobbyists can even integrate their desktop sim with virtual air traffic control to practice instrument scans and radio calls from home, saving money on aircraft rentals and instructor hours.

Fuel costs, aircraft rental fees, and safety hazards are eliminated while practicing at home, providing aspiring pilots with a limitless number of opportunities to grasp ideas in a safe setting. While flying with an instructor, students can repeat a navigation exercise or reset an approach without worrying about running out of time or money on aviation fuel. A student pilot who intends to fly an A320 or 737 in the future can also learn airline standard operating procedures by practicing with high-fidelity add-ons at home.

When aspiring pilots practice with real procedures, disciplined home simulation offers significant educational and financial benefits. A single upfront purchase of home software allows students to practice endlessly without fuel or maintenance fees, accelerating progress for instrument students practicing approaches and beginners learning switch layouts months before their first flight. Basic training aircraft and flight instructors can cost up to $200 per hour. While casual, unguided play can encourage staring at cockpit screens rather than watching outside for traffic and the horizon in trainers like the Cessna 172 or Piper Archer, following real-world checklists and using virtual reality or emerging mixed-reality interfaces that align virtual switches with physical cockpit mockups reinforce accurate visual scanning and spatial awareness.

While bridging the physical gap to actual aircraft, well-considered hardware selections further improve the training value of home installations. While real flight controls become heavier as airspeed increases and airline emergencies, like an engine failure on a Boeing 737 MAX 8 at takeoff decision speed, require 80 pounds (36 kilograms) of rudder pressure to keep the jet straight, standard desktop yokes rely on simple springs with constant tension. Pairing force-feedback controls with immersive headsets creates realistic scan patterns and cockpit familiarity before boarding an aircraft, even if light plastic pedals cannot match that heavy resistance.

Within clear regulatory guidelines, home software serves as a productive complement to accredited flight instruction. Although personal computer hours do not count toward a commercial pilot license or airline transport rating, because the Federal Aviation Administration requires certified training devices to feature enclosed cockpits, physical switches, and tested aerodynamic software, arriving at the airport with established procedural knowledge, which allows flight students to focus paid aircraft hours on better handling and maneuver practice.

You cannot learn to fly a commercial jet using Microsoft Flight Simulator alone, because aviation regulators prohibit logging personal computer hours toward official pilot certificates, and home setups lack the physical motion and control feedback of Level D sims. What you can do at home is master the exact layout of a Boeing 737, like PMDG offers, or an Airbus A320 cockpit, as Fenix made, rehearse standard checklists, and build deep familiarity with how the aircraft systems interact and behave. Practicing 'switchology' and flight computer use removes the early confusion of an unfamiliar flight deck, so students are not held back by basic button-hunting in formal training.

When a licensed pilot advances toward complex, multi-engine, or transport-category ratings, or during instrument training, this type of preparation becomes extremely beneficial. Trainees arrive already familiar with the cockpit environment and operating logic, saving costly simulator or instructor time spent recalling switch locations or automation mode responses. Long before your first actual flight, a complicated aircraft flight deck becomes a familiar workspace thanks to a solid baseline that helps you learn advanced flying skills faster, perform better during assessments, and reach career milestones with greater confidence.

The real differences between flying the Airbus A320 lineup and the Boeing 737 family show up inside the cockpit in MSFS, not on the ramp. When you load a 737 Next Generation or 737 MAX add-on, you enter a traditional flight deck with physical trim wheels that spin noisily next to your knee, manual control yokes, and overhead panels full of toggle switches you must operate manually.

A side-mounted joystick, push-button overhead panels, and intelligent fly-by-wire computers automatically trim the aircraft and prevent you from banking or tilting too far. Making the switch to an Airbus A320ceo or A320neo is like stepping into a fully automated digital workstation. In Microsoft Flight Simulator, switching between a Boeing 737 and an Airbus A320 allows users to fly an airliner from your desk in two entirely different ways.

In the 737, pilots use a center yoke, flip rows of mechanical toggle switches on the overhead panel, and watch the trim wheels beside your seat spin to change pitch. Moving to the A320 feels like entering a modern digital workspace, where you steer with a side-mounted joystick, tap illuminated push-buttons that remain dark when everything is normal, and let the fly-by-wire computers trim the jet and keep sim pilots from banking or pitching beyond safe limits.

Our Flight Tracker is now embeddable, letting any site display live flight data instead of a screenshot. Here's how to add it in three easy steps.

High-quality third-party add-ons capture the day-to-day cockpit differences, even down to the slightest button click or computer menu. You'll see firsthand how Boeing expects pilots to be hands-on with manual thrust changes and step-by-step checklist routines, whereas Airbus automates common duties using flight guidance modes and centralized electronic warning screens. Exploring both flight decks at home offers students and aviation enthusiasts a pleasant, low-cost way to learn two distinct cockpit philosophies without leaving their seats.

Beyond the cockpit switches, the simulator's realistic airport layouts and intricate global landscape allow you to practice flying both aircraft in crowded, realistic airspace. Users can load up complicated hubs like New York JFK, London Heathrow, or Tokyo Haneda to learn about standard instrument departure paths, runway markings, and complex taxiway layouts. Student pilots and hobbyists can gain a good understanding of how a Boeing and an Airbus handle cockpit workload during taxi, takeoff, and climb by practicing these ground and departure routines at home.

Comparing both aircraft families side by side on your home computer also highlights how two different design philosophies tackle the exact same airline routes. While Boeing relies on pilots to stay closely involved with manual thrust and trim adjustments during phase changes, Airbus automates much of the routine workload through flight guidance modes and centralized electronic warning screens. Exploring both cockpits in the simulator lets you experience how each manufacturer approaches automation, navigation, and pilot workload, helping you understand why airline crews train so differently for each jet.

A home flight simulator transforms abstract concepts into something you can see, test, and comprehend in real time for anyone studying professional aviation and aerospace. Entering a virtual Boeing 737 or Airbus A320 lets you see how the aircraft behaves step by step when a written explanation of a complicated procedure, flight maneuver, or aerodynamic idea seems unclear on paper. In contrast to a commercial full-motion simulator that charges hundreds of dollars per hour and adheres to a rigid curriculum, your own setup allows you the flexibility to stop, go back, and try new things anytime you feel curious.

Airbus and Boeing aircraft are built from the ground up with different design philosophies that completely change what it's like to fly them.

Enjoying the freedom to experiment, test ideas, and push buttons at home is one of the best ways to bring aviation studies to life, as long as you use it as a visual sandbox for learning how the systems think rather than a substitute for feeling a real airplane fly. You can try a steep approach, shut off a hydraulic system, or start an engine fire at takeoff speed to see how the flight computers and control surfaces respond.

This can make complex study topics understandable in a straightforward, free, and genuinely enjoyable way. In ways no actual pilot would ever take, home simulation lets students and aviation enthusiasts explore the limits of an airliner's performance envelope outside scheduled study sessions. Load a Boeing 737 MAX or Airbus A320neo to maximum weight, simulate a strong crosswind, then land on a short mountain runway to evaluate how the brakes and spoilers handle the energy.

MSFS also allows for insane, impossible stunts like max-performance vertical climbs or forceful low-altitude twists to see what happens when you go beyond real-world boundaries. Experimenting this way develops curiosity into real insight about energy management, stall speeds, and why airline operating restrictions exist in the first place. While you test those ideas, it's helpful to remember where the screen ends, and actual flight begins.

The physical seat-of-the-pants feedback of a genuine jet, such as the forceful pushback on the rudder pedals after an engine failure, the heavy airframe shudder prior to a stall, or actual G-forces pressing you into your seat, cannot be replicated. During a simulated malfunction, a desktop simulator performs a fantastic job of displaying warning lights, Master Caution bells, and flight manual numbers. This also helps develop mental habits for seeing problems early.

Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points

Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT."

If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

#6200. Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

It’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and said she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time…

I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

#6198. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then quickly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

After the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

In this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

#6196. JetBlue Launches 8 New Routes From New No.1 Airport: See Full List Now

JetBlue Airways quickly expanded its presence in markets affected by Spirit Airlines' collapse earlier this year. One airport where it has significantly increased operations is South Florida's Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL). According to schedule data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, it is now JetBlue's busiest airport by scheduled departures, overtaking John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS).

During peak periods this winter, the airline expects to offer more than 150 daily departures, marking its largest schedule ever at the airport. The carrier has already added several destinations to its network from Fort Lauderdale in recent months, and further additions are planned for next year.

JetBlue recently announced plans to introduce two new daily nonstop international routes from Fort Lauderdale, serving Comayagua, Honduras, and George Town, Cayman Islands. The Honduras service will operate to Palmerola International Airport (XPL), which serves the capital, Tegucigalpa, while flights to Grand Cayman will operate to Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM).

Comayagua will be an entirely new destination for the airline and its second in Honduras. The two additions will bring the airline's international network from Fort Lauderdale to 20 destinations. In addition, JetBlue will operate daily nonstop flights to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, for a limited period.

Complements its existing Honduran service to San Pedro Sula

To serve demand around the Trinidad and Tobago Carnival

Marked JetBlue's return to Columbus; previously served October 2006 until January 2008 from JFK and BOS

Features JetBlue's Mint lie-flat business class cabin on the cross-country route

It is very evident that JetBlue has been expanding into Spirit's former international network from Fort Lauderdale. Both of its newly announced routes to Honduras and the Cayman Islands were previously served by the ultra-low-cost carrier. The same applies to the new Colombian routes that it launched in October.

In fact, before ceasing operations in May, Spirit was the largest US airline operating in Colombia, serving seven cities from Fort Lauderdale. JetBlue quickly moved into these markets. Just two days after the airline's shutdown, it announced plans to introduce daily flights to Barranquilla's Ernesto Cortissoz International Airport (BAQ) and Cali's Alfonso Bonilla Aragón International Airport (CLO), complementing its existing services to Medellín and Cartagena.

Current Nonstop Airlines (as of Nov 2026)

Yes, but via Houston Intercontinental (stopped in 2020)

Notably, JetBlue's expansion into these former markets is not limited to international routes. The airline also introduced nonstop services from Fort Lauderdale to John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH), Indianapolis International Airport (IND) and San Diego International Airport (SAN) this month. All three routes were previously served by Spirit.

JetBlue is doubling down at FLL just as Spirit Airlines is forced to pull back.

These are just the latest additions to JetBlue's network from the South Florida airport. The airline has also introduced several new routes in previous months. In July alone, it launched eight routes, including daily services to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT), Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston, Nashville International Airport (BNA), and Mercedita International Airport (PSE) in Ponce, Puerto Rico.

JetBlue is now the largest airline at Fort Lauderdale in terms of scheduled departures, and its growth is reflected in the latest schedule figures. According to Cirium data, the carrier has scheduled more than 3,900 flights from the airport this month, up about 57% from November last year.

The expansion is even more apparent in its overall winter schedule. JetBlue has scheduled approximately 21,500 departures from Fort Lauderdale for the winter 2026/27 season, compared to nearly 13,700 during the previous winter. Its nonstop network has also grown from 47 destinations in winter 2025/26 to 62 this season.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate plans to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

#6194. Mexico’s President Flew 21 Hours To China In Economy (In A Middle Seat!)

I’ve gotta say, huge kudos to Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, for setting quite the example in terms of how she recently traveled to China, as flagged by View from the Wing…

World leaders have just met in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting. As you’d expect, most leaders flew on their government planes. There were some exceptions, though I can’t imagine anyone else flew the same way as Mexico’s 64-year-old president.

Viajamos hacia Shenzhen para representar a México en el Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC) China 2026; la agenda de actividades incluye reunión con empresarios de países miembros. Además, participaré en la conferencia de prensa matutina para informar avances de… pic.twitter.com/F9UqRLjFlb

Media reports suggest she flew to China on China Southern. Specifically, she traveled on Sunday, November 15, 2026, on CZ8032, from Mexico City (MEX) to Shenzhen (SZX), with a refueling stop in Tijuana (TIJ), and the journey covering a distance of 8,803 miles.

The Airbus A350-900 took off from Mexico City at 12:49AM, arriving in Tijuana at 2:02AM, after a flight time of 3hr13min. Then it took off again at 4:34AM, and landed in Shenzhen the following morning at 11:31AM, after a flight time of 14hr56min. All-in-all, the flight took around 21 hours, including the refueling stop.

The shocking thing here isn’t that she traveled commercial, but instead, that she reportedly flew in economy! Reports suggest she was in seat 33B, which would be a middle seat in economy, no less!

Llegamos a la Ciudad de México en el vuelo CZ8031 desde Shenzhen, China. Agradecemos a toda la tripulación por su apoyo. pic.twitter.com/DSC83CpnDQ

I think a head of state should reasonably be able to fly business class on a flight of this length, for two reasons:

That being said, I absolutely commend her for the example she is setting. It’s certainly quite a contrast to what we’ve seen here, where President Trump accepted a Boeing 747-8 as a gift from Qatar, and talked about how he has done it to make Americans be proud, because “our country has to be represented properly.” Heck, just this week he talked about “China was very impressed” and “Russia was very impressed” of his new plane. Lovely, I’m happy we’re impressing Putin, that makes me proud to be an American!

"Russia was very impressed" — Trump leads his press conference by bragging about taking the longest flight in Air Force One history, in case you were worried that he actually accomplished something useful on his trip pic.twitter.com/dDIHg8wb1w

Keep in mind that Mexico has an interesting history when it comes to how leaders fly. In 2016, Mexico’s government took control of a private Boeing 787, which flew around former President Enrique Pena Nieto. The purchase of the plane had actually been arranged under the previous president, Felipe Calderón, in 2012.

Then in 2018, when Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador took charge in Mexico, he fulfilled a campaign promise of selling that 787, which turned out to be pretty challenging, given that demand for a secondhand VIP 787 isn’t exactly that high (the plane ended up going to Tajikistan). Sheinbaum has kept that general legacy going, by flying commercial.

Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, traveled to the recent summit in China differently than virtually all other government leaders. Not only did she fly commercial, but she traveled in economy, and reportedly even in a middle seat.

There’s no denying that this is more about optics than anything, but I very much respect that. It’s nice to see heads of state who lead by example, as it’s pretty rare to see nowadays.

What do you make of Sheinbaum’s travel style?

This is so performative and dumb. Hope she gets voted out.

Does China Southern offer wi-fi on its A350s? Hard to believe that the head of state of a country like Mexico would be out of reach for 21 hours.

Well, either she is a believer in living as the people do, or she’s a very smart politician whom knows humility is rare and appreciated these days… both options earn my praise.

#6193. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6192. Why All 3 Of Boeing's Most Modern Aircraft Have Drastically Different Wingtip Designs

Boeing's three most modern commercial aircraft, the Boeing 737 MAX, Boeing 787 Dreamliner, and Boeing 777X, share a common objective when it comes to their wing designs: reducing aerodynamic drag and improving fuel efficiency. However, despite pursuing the same goal, all three aircraft feature noticeably different wingtip designs, ranging from distinctive split-tip winglets to swept-back extensions and even enormous folding wingtips.

The differences are not simply a matter of appearance or Boeing experimenting with alternative technologies. Instead, each design reflects a combination of aerodynamic performance, aircraft dimensions, and the practical limitations imposed by airports. Understanding why these aircraft have such different wingtips provides an interesting insight into the compromises involved in modern aircraft engineering.

An aircraft's wingtips play an important role in determining how efficiently it flies, particularly during cruise. As air moves around a wing, higher-pressure air beneath the wing attempts to move toward the lower-pressure region above it. This movement creates swirling vortices around the wingtips, which contribute to a phenomenon known as induced drag. The resulting resistance makes it harder for an aircraft to maintain speed and requires additional engine thrust.

Reducing induced drag is therefore a major consideration when manufacturers design new commercial aircraft. One of the most straightforward ways to achieve this is by increasing the wingspan, effectively distributing lift across a longer wing and reducing the strength of the vortices produced at its extremities. However, making wings longer introduces another challenge, since airports have strict limits on how much space aircraft can occupy.

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) establishes aircraft size categories that help airports determine which aircraft can use particular gates, taxiways, and other infrastructure. These categories are largely determined by wingspan, meaning manufacturers cannot simply make every aircraft's wings as long as they would ideally like. An aircraft that exceeds the relevant dimensions could require different airport facilities, potentially limiting its operational flexibility.

Boeing's engineers must consequently balance aerodynamic efficiency against the practical requirements of commercial aviation. Different wingtip devices offer different ways to manage this compromise. Some extend the effective wing vertically, while others increase the actual wingspan or combine both approaches. The three aircraft demonstrate how these engineering decisions can produce substantially different solutions to essentially the same aerodynamic problem.

The Boeing 737 MAX features perhaps the most visually distinctive wingtip arrangement of the three aircraft. Its Advanced Technology winglets have two separate extensions, with one pointing upward and another extending downward. This split-tip configuration gives the aircraft a distinctive appearance while helping reduce induced drag without requiring a substantial increase in its overall wingspan.

The reason Boeing selected this particular arrangement becomes clearer when considering the aircraft's relationship with the 737 Next Generation family. The Boeing 737 MAX was developed to retain considerable operational commonality with its predecessors, allowing airlines to introduce the newer aircraft without requiring significant changes to their existing airport infrastructure. Keeping its wingspan within the ICAO Code C limit of 118 feet (36 meters) was therefore an important design consideration.

A conventional raked wingtip, such as the arrangement found on the Boeing 787, would have extended the 737 MAX's wings too far horizontally. This could have pushed the aircraft outside the dimensions associated with its existing airport category, creating complications for airlines operating it alongside older 737 variants. The split-tip design improved aerodynamic performance while keeping the aircraft within its required dimensional limits.

The winglets also incorporate carefully shaped surfaces designed to manage airflow and reduce aerodynamic losses. Rather than simply adding extensions to the existing wing, Boeing developed a more sophisticated arrangement intended to improve overall efficiency. This was particularly important for an aircraft that needed to deliver better fuel economy while retaining much of the operational flexibility that had made earlier 737 generations attractive to airlines.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that Southwest Airlines is currently the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737 MAX, with a total of 300 in its fleet, followed by United Airlines with 243.

Boeing has achieved its first target for MAX deliveries, but is still working to reach the higher rate of 47 deliveries a month.

Unlike the 737 MAX, the Boeing 787 was developed as an entirely new aircraft family, giving Boeing considerably more freedom when designing its wings. Rather than adopting conventional vertical winglets, the manufacturer opted for long, swept-back raked wingtips that extend the wing horizontally. The result is a particularly elegant design that contributes to the 787's distinctive appearance.

The Boeing 787's wing design was developed with aerodynamic efficiency as a central priority, rather than being constrained by the dimensional requirements associated with an existing narrowbody aircraft family. Its larger wingspan allows the aircraft to benefit from the reduced induced drag associated with longer wings. Boeing was therefore able to pursue a solution that offered aerodynamic advantages without introducing conventional upward-pointing winglets.

Research from Boeing and NASA indicates that raked wingtips can reduce drag by approximately 5.5%, compared with improvements of around 3.5% to 4.5% for conventional winglets. Although the precise benefits depend on the aircraft and operating conditions, these figures help explain why Boeing selected this configuration for its widebody aircraft. The design also avoids some of the additional structural weight associated with separate winglet structures.

United Airlines is currently the world's largest operator of the Boeing 787, as outlined in the table below:

Another important characteristic of the Boeing 787's wings is their composite construction. Built primarily from advanced carbon-fiber-reinforced materials, they are designed to be long, relatively thin, and flexible. This flexibility allows the wings to respond to aerodynamic forces during flight, while their overall shape contributes to improved efficiency. Combined with the raked wingtips, the design helps the 787 achieve the aerodynamic performance required for long-distance commercial operations.

The Boeing 777X takes the concept of longer wings considerably further, featuring the largest wingspan of any commercial airliner currently designed for airline service. Its wings extend 235 feet (72 meters) when fully deployed. This substantial span helps reduce induced drag and supports the aircraft's objective of delivering improved fuel efficiency on long-haul routes.

However, the Boeing 777X faces a practical problem that the 787 does not encounter to the same extent. Its enormous wingspan would exceed the dimensions permitted within the ICAO Code E category used by many large commercial aircraft. This could make it difficult for the aircraft to operate at airports designed around the existing infrastructure used by conventional widebody aircraft, potentially restricting where airlines could deploy it.

Boeing's solution was to develop folding wingtips that allow the outer sections of the wings to rotate upward while the aircraft is on the ground. Once folded, the 777X's wingspan is reduced to just under 213 feet (65 m), bringing it within the dimensional requirements associated with Code E airport operations. Before take-off, the wingtips extend into their normal flight positions, restoring the aircraft's full aerodynamic configuration.

This arrangement is particularly interesting because it allows Boeing to avoid choosing between aerodynamic performance and airport compatibility. The aircraft can benefit from an exceptionally long wing during flight without requiring airports to accommodate its entire wingspan while parked or taxiing. The folding mechanism adds engineering complexity, but it provides a practical solution to a problem that would otherwise have required substantial compromises in wing design.

This innovative design feature has captured global attention.

The Boeing 777X is set to become the latest and largest member of the manufacturer's successful 777 family. Designed to offer improved efficiency, greater range, and increased passenger comfort, the aircraft will be available in three variants: the 777-8 and 777-9 passenger models, along with the 777-8F cargo aircraft. The Boeing 777-9 will be the first variant to enter service, offering airlines a high-capacity long-haul aircraft. The smaller 777-8 will provide greater range, while the freighter version targets the growing cargo market.

However, the program has experienced considerable delays. Originally expected to enter service in 2020, the Boeing 777X has faced certification challenges, flight-testing setbacks, and issues involving its new GE9X engines. As of November 2026, Boeing is targeting the first 777-9 delivery in 2027. The 777-8F is expected around two years later, while the passenger 777-8 is not anticipated before 2030. Despite the setbacks, the 777X remains an important part of Boeing's future long-haul aircraft plans.

Emirates is set to be the world's largest operator of the Boeing 777X, with a staggering 270 on order. The carriers with the largest firm orders for the passenger variants of the 777X (777-8 and 777-9) are outlined in the table below:

Although the three Boeing aircraft use different solutions, their wingtip designs are based on the same aerodynamic principles. All three aim to reduce induced drag, improve lift distribution, and lower the amount of energy required to maintain efficient flight. The differences emerge because each aircraft operates within a different set of dimensional and engineering constraints, rather than because Boeing has changed its overall approach to aerodynamic efficiency.

For the Boeing 737 MAX, airport compatibility was particularly important because the aircraft needed to retain the operational flexibility of the previous 737 generation. Its split-tip winglets provide aerodynamic improvements without substantially increasing its wingspan, making them a practical solution for a narrowbody aircraft operating across a wide variety of airports.

The Boeing 787 had greater design freedom, allowing Boeing to prioritize aerodynamic performance through a longer wing and swept-back raked wingtips. Its composite construction also makes it possible to develop a lightweight, flexible wing structure that works particularly well with this configuration. The absence of conventional winglets is therefore a deliberate engineering decision, not an omission.

Meanwhile, the Boeing 777X represents a different approach altogether, combining the aerodynamic advantages of an exceptionally long wing with a folding mechanism that addresses airport limitations. Its design demonstrates how manufacturers can use mechanical innovation to overcome restrictions that would otherwise prevent them from pursuing more ambitious aerodynamic improvements.

Together, these three aircraft show that there is no single ideal wingtip design for every commercial aircraft, since the most effective solution ultimately depends on the aircraft's size, intended operations, and the infrastructure it must use.

#6191. Why JSX Just Bought New Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

Let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

Then there’s New Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business plan was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

The business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

That brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

JSX acquires New Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy

On the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. New Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

Long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a company that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

Going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

Under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with New Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

If the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

JSX has just bought New Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have plans to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?
